items.answer: Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.

Original graph is the weighted graph input to an optimal-path algorithm that represents a virtual world, with vertices as points of interest, directly connected edges weighted by Euclidean distance, connected but not necessarily complete, and importance and waiting time specified for each node.

Time threshold (TTH) is the maximum duration of user movement, experience, or virtual reality exposure in a virtual tour, beyond which cybersickness may occur; it is the upper time limit used when optimizing a tour path.

items.prompt: What is vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP)?
items.answer: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem, an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit, the importance of the nodes, within a time constraint.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

questions.question: What remains a problem with the optimal path approach in a very large virtual world?
options: Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the minimum point count
Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the maximum walking speed
Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the display frame budget
Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the safe exposure duration
questions.explanation: Finding the shortest route through all points does not guarantee that the tour fits the user's safe VR exposure time; in a large world the minimum time can still be too long and cause cybersickness.

questions.question: How does the optimal path under a time constraint differ from the basic optimal path approach?
options: It adds an upper distance limit and a goal of covering the most important points within it
It adds an upper speed limit and a goal of covering every point within it
It adds an upper point limit and a goal of covering the least important points within it
It adds an upper exposure limit and a goal of covering the most important points within it
questions.explanation: The time-constrained approach sets a maximum exposure time and then chooses a path that fits that time while covering as many important points as possible, instead of merely finding the shortest path through all points.

questions.question: Why is a complete walking-based tour of Auniati's whole site not recommended as a VR experience?
options: A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can induce cybersickness
A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can improve spatial memory
A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can reduce the need for navigation
A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can increase walking realism
questions.explanation: A full walk of the site may take as long as a day, and such a long VR exposure is not advised because it can induce cybersickness.

questions.question: Why does the system-controlled Auniati VR tour use a natural walking speed model?
options: To make every point of interest more important
To make the walking-based exploration feel realistic
To make the shortest navigation path shorter
To make the time threshold easier to satisfy
questions.explanation: The tour keeps walking-based exploration realistic by using a natural walking speed model; the model is for realism, not for changing the path length, threshold, or point importance.

data.text: The Majuli VR tour must control how long users are exposed to a large virtual site, because Auniati Satra is big enough that a full walk can be unsafe in VR. Since the tour uses walking-based exploration at a natural walking speed, the navigation path directly affects exposure time. The optimal path approach may still take too long, so the time-constrained approach limits exposure by choosing which important points can be covered within a set time.
points: Majuli is a river island, and Auniati Satra has at least 25 points of interest.
Exploring all of Auniati Satra by walking can take up to a day, and full-day VR exposure would induce cybersickness.
The system-controlled Auniati Satra VR tour uses walking-based exploration with a natural walking speed model.
The optimal path approach finds the minimum-time route covering all points, but in Majuli it may still cause cybersickness.
The time-constrained approach sets an exposure threshold and covers the most important points within that limit.

questions.question: Which value is used as the edge weight between two point-of-interest nodes in the Satra campus graph?
options: The walking time between the two point-of-interest locations
The importance score at the two point-of-interest locations
The maximum wait time at the two point-of-interest locations
The Euclidean distance between the two point-of-interest locations
questions.explanation: In the Satra graph, edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the points of interest they connect. Importance and wait time are attributes associated with points of interest, not with edges.

questions.question: When are per-point importance values and maximum wait times required in the Satra VR navigation optimization?
options: When the proposed route has to skip the lake corners because of distance
When the all-point minimum-time path is longer than the exposure time threshold
When the campus graph has fewer than the stated minimum number of nodes
When the field study relied only on interviews with Satra committee members
questions.explanation: The second optimization approach is needed when the shortest route through all points of interest still takes too long for a comfortable VR exposure. Then points of interest are ranked by importance and their stopping times are included so that the best route can be found within the time limit.

questions.question: How was the field-study data for the Satra graph gathered?
options: By extracting preexisting map coordinates and comparing them with satellite views at the Satra
By asking remote users to rate a fixed list of landmarks at the Satra
By testing a finished virtual tour and recording comfort reports at the Satra
By observing visitors' movement and stopping and interviewing residents at the Satra
questions.explanation: The graph was built from on-site contextual inquiry: people's travel and stopping behavior were observed and manually recorded, and campus residents and Satra committee members were interviewed about places people visit and recommend.

questions.question: What does the maximum wait time at a point of interest cover in the navigation model?
options: Time to pause, calibrate, and restart the virtual session before resuming navigation
Time to choose, compare, and preview the next stop before resuming navigation
Time to walk, look around, and take photographs before resuming navigation
Time to stop, inspect, and interact with the place before resuming navigation
questions.explanation: Maximum wait time is the time needed at a point of interest for the user to stop, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and then continue navigating. It is not the time spent traveling to the next point or performing system setup.

data.text: Turning the Majuli Satra site into a weighted point-of-interest graph enables routing solvers to optimize navigation. The graph is built from field study, and when a simple minimum-time route is too long, a second approach adds POI importance and maximum wait time. A TSP solver can cover all POIs, while a VRPP solver can choose a route within a time limit that favors the most important POIs.
points: The Satra graph has at least 25 point-of-interest nodes, Euclidean-distance edges, and POIs need not be physical.
The Satra graph is built iteratively through field study, observing travel behavior and interviewing residents and committee members.
If the first path exceeds the time threshold, the second approach assigns each POI importance and maximum wait time.
A POI's maximum wait time is the time to stop, inspect, interact, and resume navigation.
Using the graph, TSP finds a minimum-time all-node path; VRPP finds a threshold path maximizing important POIs.

questions.question: Why can the optimal path approach for a virtual reality navigation route still be unsuitable for the Auniati Satra tour even though it minimizes travel time?
questions.reference_answer: The optimal path approach finds the minimum-time path that lets a user explore all points of interest. In a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time can still be very large compared with the expected virtual reality exposure duration. Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking may take up to a day, and a full-day virtual reality exposure is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness.

questions.question: How does the optimal path under a time constraint approach use the time threshold to choose a navigation path for a walking-based virtual reality tour of Auniati Satra?
questions.reference_answer: The approach sets an upper exposure limit, the time threshold, and searches for a path only within that duration. It selects the path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting them and navigating between them. Keeping the tour within this threshold matters because exceeding it may cause cybersickness.

questions.question: Why must points of interest in the time-constrained virtual reality navigation model be assigned relative importance and maximum wait time before a vehicle routing problem with profit solver is used?
questions.reference_answer: The time-constrained virtual reality navigation model requires each point of interest to have relative importance and maximum wait time. Importance is the profit a vehicle routing problem with profit route maximizes within a time constraint, and wait time is the time to stop, inspect, interact if possible, and resume navigation. These let the solver keep the route within the time threshold, accounting for stopping time, while covering the most important points.
